kingdom-in-the-sky.title: Kingdom in the sky
kingdom-in-the-sky.intro: An epic two-week journey across the vast & majestic mountain kingdom of Lesotho. From Qacha’s nek, through the heart of Semonkong. Across Thaba Tseka through the hidden mountain villages of Mohlanapeng and Mokhotlong. This is a deeply traditional world free from the entrapment of modernity, I witnessed gentle welcoming people embrace a harsh environment living above 3000 meters. The visual process: Working primarily in the darkroom Willman produces one-of-a-kind silver gelatin prints. Each work is hand-crafted and unrepeatable, resisting the conventions of editioned analogue photography and positioning the photograph as a singular object. Alongside his analogue practice, Willman’s digital works extend similar concerns with perception, scale, and temporality, while remaining grounded in a disciplined visual language. His work is exhibited internationally and is held in private and institutional collections. Willman lives and works in South Africa.

last-of-the-san-bushmen.title: Last of the San Bushmen
last-of-the-san-bushmen.intro: Across the arid lands of the Northern Cape, along endless red sand dune ridges there exist a people whose presence upon these lands have witnessed a thousand centuries never changing. Yet here, upon those forgotten lands along the dried up Auob river there is life as it has been forever. A people tied spiritually and physically to the health and wealth of these Greatlands of the Kgalagadi desert. During my precious time with the Khoi San people (bushmen) it was clear that generationally this is perhaps the last generation of Khoi San upholding and maintaining a traditional life away from western influence. Some nights when I sit alone a part of me cries. I can still hear their melodic voices sharing stories of their day with elders and children huddled around a fire, their faces shadowed by the flickering flame. With the sun long set I watch as their hand gestures along with heads adorned with antlers of tiny animals’ silhouette upon the horizon. A people whose future remains uncertain.

tuisland.title: TUISLAND ’n stillewe
tuisland.intro: ...... 35 years later I offer ‘TUISLAND, ’n Stillewe’. In so doing, I pay respects and homage through this body of work to two significant South African photographers, Paul Alberts & David Goldblatt who went out beyond the marginalized line of a once divided country to discover, record and interpret a new way of storytelling through the photographic image. An entire generation has passed since their celebrated works came to light and here now something new has emerged. Two elements in this body of work sew a golden thread connecting these two generations. First is the method of analogue film photography. The entire process for each image in this book from capturing the image, to developing the negatives to hand printing each negative in a darkroom is exactly how it was done during the pre-digital age. The meditation & method to capture and print is the twine that makes each image a work of art. The second aspect which bridges this work with our history is the privilege and recognition this collection has received from Antjie Krog herself. Beloved of her peers, respected of a generation that overcame huge odds, her foreword and deep insight is a testimony to her legacy as an author and poet. There is a seamless marriage between her message and her connection to the images themselves. A marriage of two minds. tatom-khulu-mandela.title: Tatom Khulu Mandela
tatom-khulu-mandela.intro: Perhaps one of Willman’s greatest achievements was his significant contribution to the recording of the process of South Africa’s democratic change. In 2003 Willman was commissioned to archive and document the life and times of Nelson Mandela for the Nelson Mandela Foundation. Over the years this afforded him many intimate experiences with a man who for Willman embodies the very spirit and conviction we all possess as Africans in the world today. Willman’s collection of work is now central to the Mandela Centre of Memory & Presidential Library in Johannesburg. This original handprint collection depicts just one occasion where Willman was granted private access to photograph intimate moments with Nelson Mandela. On a single roll of 35mm film Willman relied on his intuition, his passion and love for this man to capture an extraordinary collection of images. It was from this inspired photo shoot that many of the images created went on to define and build the living legacy of Nelson Mandela.

inanda-heritage-collection.title: Inanda Heritage Collection
inanda-heritage-collection.intro: Whilst those around Willman emigrated and sought refuge away from a fast-changing South Africa, Willman chose instead to pack his bags and over the winter of 2001 he began to photograph what today is the Inanda Heritage route. Spread over 60 km from the city of Pietermaritzburg to the mouth of the Umgeni river into the Indian Ocean, the Inanda valley tells the story of rural communities forging lives, creating history and building one of Africa’s largest multicultural communities. It was this collection that became Willman’s very first serious body of work that launched his career as a photographer. Willman has never followed trends but has doggedly, though out his career, followed his own desire to capture people and places that interested him and where he sought to create value as a photographer.

the-willman-collection.title: The Willman Collection
the-willman-collection.intro: The camera gives the creative eye freedom to explore, to play, to take from out the world everything that distracts and to focus in on the essence of the moment.

the-south-african-heritage-collection.title: The South African Heritage Collection
the-south-african-heritage-collection.intro: Documented over 25 years this rare original print collection details moments with extraordinary leaders, places and artifacts from out a time in South Africa when the call to freedom brought history, culture, race and faiths in South Africa to its knees. When most young South Africans chose to ignore our collective history or even emigrate, photographer Matthew Willman stepped up and chose to dive in to explore, to learn, to bring to light the reality of what happened pre-1994. With the passage of time all Willman’s peers will have passed away. In years to come with age on his side Willman’s body of work with his incredible stories, Willman will be the only living documenter able to share first hand stories and experiences of this incredible time in South Africa’s history.

the-victoria-falls-collection.title: The Victoria Falls Collection
the-victoria-falls-collection.intro: Captured over 3 separate shoots over 2 years The Victoria Falls Collection became Willman’s first analogue photo shoot without any digital assistance. This collection was exhibited for 2 years at The Royal Livingstone hotel in Zambia with most the collection either sold to patrons of the hotel or donated as part of the legacy of the mighty Zambezi and Victoria Falls.

breaking-bounds.title: Breaking Bounds
breaking-bounds.intro: Before Willman committed his life to the pursuit of photography, he was a trained ballet dancer for 20 years. It wasn’t until 12 years after he stopped actively training that Willman returned to the world of dance, but this time with his camera. With his trained eye for movement and expression Willman has created images that define the decisive moment. Between his digital creations and analogue works Willman continues to push the boundaries of creativity and human expression within the world of dance.

greatlands.title: Greatlands
greatlands.intro: This iconic body of photographic work transcends what is ordinarily perceived as beautiful, perfect or picturesque in landscape photography. Matthew Willman has created a masterpiece for the ages, presenting a deeply moving depiction of Southern Africa as it really is. The great lands here are ancient and hold memory from times long forgotten. They are scorched by the sun and weathered by the wind and rain. Over three consecutive years, Willman travelled across eight countries in Southern Africa covering 32 000 kilometres (20 000 miles) to masterfully capture on analogue film devastatingly beautiful landscapes. There is something else that whispers through these images. There echoes in each frame a memory, a painfully beautiful testimony to the pioneers who forged paths upon these roughshod lands. Men and women who made these frontiers their home and produced life across this sleeping Eden of Southern Africa. All photographs were captured using 35mm Canon A1 cameras (50mm prime lenses) and on 6x7 120 roll film on a Mamiya RB67 camera (127mm & 250mm lenses). All images were hand processed, then hand printed in the darkroom by Matthew Willman. The Greatlands collection was inspired by Jacobus Hendrik Pierneef’s monumental Southern African landscape artworks and South African author, Alan Paton.

great-zimbabwe-ruins.title: Great Zimbabwe Ruins
great-zimbabwe-ruins.intro: As a child I ran through these ancient ruins oblivious to its legacy and incredible history. A relic from a time so ancient that historians today still baffle at its true meaning and impact upon Southern Africa. 35 years later at the height of one of Zimbabwe’s driest seasons I returned to these great ruins. For weeks bellowing grey clouds passed overhead teasing the now parched and arid lands. As I moved silently alone through these majestic ruins capturing images I noticed how my shutter speed kept dropping. As I rewound the shutter advance lever on my medium format Mamiya RB 67 having captured the centre piece of the Great Ruins of Zimbabwe dark circles appeared around me covering the chiselled rocks. Finally, the first drops of rain were falling to the earth. Within moments standing within the inner sanctum of these revered ruins the heavens opened, and the clouds wept upon the lands.

the-robben-island-story.title: The Robben Island Story
the-robben-island-story.intro: A deeply moving encounter photographed over a period of 18 months documenting for the Robben Island Museum & The Nelson Mandela Museum. It was this body of work achieved between 2001 – 2003 that ultimately opened the doors to Willman’s entrance to Nelson Mandela and his subsequent 10 years photographing for the Nelson Mandela Centre of Memory.

african-child.title: African Child
african-child.intro: Willman’s art is rooted in an ongoing exploration of the human condition. It is not concerned with the extraordinary as separate from the everyday. Rather, it is in the ordinary gestures-a glance, a posture, a moment of stillness-that something profound emerges. A stillness of being, a mastery of craft within analogue photography. There emerges a reverence and dignity in each of his portrait works. Through this approach, the portraits depicted here are neither subjects nor symbols; they are individuals whose presence quietly insists on recognition. There is a deep ethic of encounter in these images. To photograph a child is to engage with a future not yet written. In this way, the work becomes both document and offering: a visual narrative of youth across Southern Africa, a meditation on continuity, resilience, and imagination. In looking at these portraits, we are not simply observing childhood-we are being asked to remember it, to reconsider it, and perhaps, to see in it the contours of a shared African humanity that is still unfolding. Willman’s practice can be read in dialogue with traditions of documentary photography while also departing from them captured as iconic and historic fine art. His work is a collector’s masterpiece with each art piece an original hand printed creation. With the artists own hand forming and shaping light and shade the negative in the darkroom becomes Willman’s distinctive work of art.

the-save-collection.title: The Savé Collection
the-save-collection.intro: The Savé Valley Conservancy is one of the largest private game reserves in Africa. Located in the Southeastern lowveld of Zimbabwe, bordering on the Save River on its eastern side, the Conservancy comprises 750,000 acres of diverse wildlife habitat. Yet along its bordering fence lines, rural village communities eke out a living adapting to the ever-changing relationship between Game Parks and surrounding communities. Working alongside Isaiah’s House, a non-profit Christian organisation based in the USA positive change is taking shape. Over 700 bore holes have been built, reservoir tanks, fences along side renovations to school classrooms and a local clinic. This collection was sold in the USA where funds raised went back into the further development of these communities.
